text: Vaccination is a key tool against endemic and severe disease, but it is never 100% effective and must be combined with good hygiene, biosecurity, and management; it is also expensive, so the disease risk and impact should be weighed before designing a vaccination program (sometimes better hygiene and housing achieve more than a costly vaccine). Selecting a vaccine requires a confirmed diagnosis first — for example, nervous symptoms/convulsions in post-weaning pigs are often wrongly attributed to Aujeszky disease, which normally causes convulsions only in newborn piglets, when Edema Disease or Streptococcus is more likely; vaccinating for the wrong disease wastes money and doesn't help. Strain matters too — a cheaper monovalent FMD vaccine (e.g. strain O only) gives no protection if the actual outbreak strain is different (e.g. Asia1), and since strain cannot be told from symptoms alone, a trivalent (O+A+Asia1) vaccine is recommended in Cambodia. Mutation can also defeat vaccines — a new highly pathogenic PRRS strain identified in 2010 was not covered by vaccines developed abroad, and using them risked introducing new virus onto farms, so PRRS vaccination is not recommended. Common causes of vaccination failure: a broken cold chain (live vaccines especially can be partially or fully inactivated above 8°C); inconsistent vaccine quality/purity; an expired vaccine; high maternal antibody levels neutralizing the vaccine (common during the suckling period, requiring a later repeat dose); vaccinating an animal already incubating the disease (which can even bring symptoms on faster); dirty injection equipment (organic matter or antibiotic traces destroy the vaccine microbes); equipment cleaned with disinfectant (even trace amounts kill live-vaccine microbes); poor injection technique (e.g. injecting sows in the mid-neck fat with too-short needles, so the vaccine stays in fat rather than reaching the muscle/bloodstream); or vaccinating an animal currently on antibiotics.
